This presumption as observed by the Appellate Division in Abani Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian (SDO) Vested Property, Chandpur and ors reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223 strongly attests to the genuineness of registered documents under section 60 of the Act. Indeed, and as was also the case in the Gangamoyi Debi Case, the matter before us also involved the element of an alleged deliberate fraud and collusion committed, an allegation that necessarily must be substantiated under stringent rules of proof and scrutiny. Of course, by virtue of Proviso 1 of section 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 oral evidence may be admitted to contradict, vary or subtract from any terms of a contract or other disposition of property reduced to the form of a document, it is nevertheless the case by reason of rules of pleadings developed by judicial authority that allegations of deceit, fraud and collusion have to be brought and framed in a particular manner. Read with Order VI, rule 4 of the Code such judicial authority stresses that general allegations, however strong the words, are insufficient to substantiate an averment of fraud. In other words, what is required are positive statements and affirmations coupled with the offer of strong and substantial evidence. That apparently is the line of reasoning adopted by the learned Senior Assistant Judge-in-Charge when considering the crucial aspect of fraud and collusion ostensibly leading to the plaintiff-opposite party affixing her left thumb impression (LTI) in execution of the Kabala. Finding that no credible or substantial evidence had been adduced by or on behalf of the plaintiff either to show and prove the nature and extent of her claimed ailment at the time, and the manner in which she may have been induced to affix her LTI several times on the Kabala in question, the trial Court came to a finding that the burden of proof required of the plaintiff-opposite party in discharge of her responsibility to prove fraud and collusion had not been so done sufficiently in keeping with standards established in long-standing judicial authority. It is in that context this Court has taken note of the reference in the trial Court's judgment to the observation on the standard of discharging the onus of proof in such circumstances as found in the case of Kiron Chandra Das vs Sirajul Hoque Patwari reported in 34 DLR 225 at paragraph 5, 226 thus: 

 "There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction as there is a presumption of innocence in criminal matters. That being so the burden of proving every species of bad faith such as fraud, collusion, misrepresentation, impersonation, undue influence, absence of consideration rests on the person who asserts the same and only after that burden was discharged prima facie the burden would shift on the other party to prove that it was not so." 

 10. It is further evident that the trial Court found that the plaintiff-opposite party had failed to satisfactorily discharge prima facie that burden of proof imposed on her by reason of a preponderance of evidence operating in favour of the defendant-petitioner in discharging his responsibility to prove the due and proper execution of the registered Kabala.
